appraisal_events.evidence: "Mais c'est moi qui lui ai fait connaître tout cela... tous les motifs qu'il a peints"; "il ne savait pas distinguer un althéa d'une passe-rose", "Il n'a jamais su faire un bouquet", "On ne l'appelait chez nous que Monsieur Tiche", "s'il n'avait pas fait ce sale mariage"; the diarist concludes that without her he might never have known how to paint a jasmine.
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Verdurin claims the substance of Elstir's art as her own gift to him and belittles the man, and the memorialist takes the claim at face value — a credulity the outer narration has already marked as naive.

appraisal_events.evidence: Cottard speaks "avec une finesse qui décèle chez lui l'homme tout à fait distingué", cites the burnt valet "d'une façon vraiment plus philosophique que ne feraient bien des médecins", and flatly overrides Swann on Napoleon's books: "ces taches ne viennent pas du tout de cela — mais là, pas du tout — insiste-t-il avec autorité".
appraisal_events.explanation: The journal makes Cottard the evening's penetrating mind and lets him close the argument over Swann, an elevation the framing narration flatly contradicts by recalling how insipid and common these same people seemed in life.

appraisal_events.evidence: "À mon nom prononcé par Verdurin, il n'a pas une parole qui marque qu'il connaisse nos livres", read as "cette conspiration qu'organise contre nous la Sorbonne... l'hostilité d'un silence voulu"; the diarist retaliates by painting Brichot with a butler's whiskers, retailing second-form jokes with condescension.
appraisal_events.explanation: Recognition is pointedly withheld from the guest of honour in the salon where he is feted, and the wound is reported by the wounded party in terms the frame invites us to discount.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Je ne m'étais jamais dissimulé que je ne savais pas écouter ni... regarder ; une vieille femme ne montrait à mes yeux aucune espèce de collier de perles"; the same Verdurin, Cottard and Guermantes he had dined with had seemed to him nothing but "vulgarités sans nombre" — "Et que tout cela fît un astre dans la nuit !!!"
appraisal_events.explanation: The Goncourt page painfully demonstrates the narrator's incapacity to see and hear, and his own defence of a different, radiographic faculty is offered only provisionally.

status_effects.explanation: Within the journal his originality is reduced to what a hostess taught him, down to recognizing jasmine, and he is remembered as the household's "Monsieur Tiche".
The memorialist credits her with the motifs, the flowers and even the conception of Elstir's great portrait, making her the origin of a celebrated art.
He holds the table across three subjects, is credited with philosophical penetration, and has the last authoritative word.
His erudite explanation of the stains on Napoleon's books is contradicted outright by Cottard, who supplies the accepted version.
Deference is visibly withheld from him at the table where he is otherwise feted: the academic will not acknowledge his books.
The portrait the journal returns for the snub is wholly deflating: a maître d'hôtel's face and a schoolmaster's condescending pleasantries.
He is left troubled and diminished before a page that turned into a star the very evenings he had found insipid.

ambiguities: Almost the whole passage is a pastiche of the Goncourt journal being read by the narrator, so every appraisal inside it is staged at one remove and is explicitly qualified by the framing remark on "l'indice individuel de naïveté qui est frappant chez le mémorialiste".
That Brichot's silence was deliberate is asserted only by the aggrieved diarist, so the snub may be his vanity rather than a witnessed act.
